title: Indian Student Visas to the U.S. Drop 60 Percent as Trump Tightens F-1 Rules
excerpt: A new DHS rule ending open-ended student stays takes effect September 15, capping F-1 visas at four years and slashing the post-graduation grace period in half.
body:
• F-1 student visas issued to Indian applicants fell 60% between May and August 2025 compared to 2017, according to a Center for Immigration Studies analysis released this week.
  • A finalized DHS rule taking effect September 15, 2026 replaces the decades-old "duration of status" system with a strict four-year cap on F-1, J-1, and I visas.
  • The post-completion grace period drops from 60 to 30 days, and graduate students can no longer switch majors or transfer schools without federal approval.
  • India is the largest source country for F-1 students in the U.S., with more than 330,000 Indian students currently enrolled.

The number of F-1 student visas issued to Indian applicants has dropped 60 percent since the Trump administration began its crackdown on foreign students, according to a Center for Immigration Studies analysis released this week. The decline far outpaces the 46 percent drop among Chinese applicants over the same period.

Chinese and Indian students together make up 53 percent of all foreign students enrolled in U.S. higher education. The plunge comes as a sweeping new Department of Homeland Security rule — finalized on July 16 and set to take effect September 15, 2026 — fundamentally restructures how international students are admitted and monitored in the country.

What the New Rule Changes

The regulation eliminates "duration of status," the framework that since 1978 allowed F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, and I-visa media professionals to remain in the U.S. for as long as their program lasted, without a fixed end date on their immigration paperwork.

Under the new system, student and exchange visas carry a hard four-year maximum. Anyone needing more time — including the majority of Ph.D. candidates, whose programs routinely exceed four years — must file a formal extension with USCIS and undergo biometric vetting, background checks, and fraud screening.

The rule also cuts the post-completion grace period from 60 days to 30 days, giving graduates half the time to apply for Optional Practical Training, change status, or prepare to leave. Graduate students can no longer change their stated educational objective or transfer to another institution without securing prior federal authorization.

"International students, many of whom will have spent years in the USA, will now have just 30 days to find an employer to sponsor them or immediately be turned into illegal immigrants. Have these people no understanding of how life works?"

— David J. Bier, Director of Immigration Studies, Cato Institute

Why Indian Students Bear the Biggest Impact

India surpassed China in 2023 as the largest source country for F-1 students in the U.S., with more than 330,000 Indian nationals currently enrolled in American universities. That makes Indian students the single largest group exposed to the practical mechanics of this shift.

Students already in the country on a duration-of-status basis will transition automatically into the new fixed-period system, with their authorized stay capped at four years from the rule's effective date. No fresh paperwork is required immediately, but the clock starts ticking on September 15.

The Trump administration has also proposed a $100,000 fee for foreign graduates who want to remain in the U.S. and work after completing their degrees — a measure that, if implemented, would price out most Indian applicants pursuing post-study work authorization.

Backlash From Education Leaders

The proposal received nearly 22,000 public comments, the vast majority opposing the changes. International education organizations have pushed back sharply since the rule was finalized.

Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, called it "a misguided and unnecessary policy shift that injects uncertainty, bureaucracy, and fear into a system that has long worked effectively." The American Immigration Lawyers Association said the rule "duplicates processes already managed through SEVIS" and is part of a broader effort to dismantle the legal immigration system.

Critics also point to USCIS's existing backlog of over 11.65 million cases, with average processing times exceeding one year. Requiring millions of extension filings could overwhelm an already strained system and leave students in limbo — unsure whether they can continue their education while their applications are pending.

"If they're going to be very strict on 'We're only going to give very limited cases after four years,' then we're going to lose a lot of graduate students. That's the reality, because not all programs are going to be able to adjust to that."

— Delo Blough, Retired Director of International Services

The Administration's Case

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the rule, arguing that the old system allowed "thousands to abuse our immigration system by perpetually enrolling in courses to avoid having to leave the U.S." The department cited 2,100 international students admitted between 2000 and 2010 who remain in F-1 status more than 15 years later.

George Fishman of the Center for Immigration Studies echoed the administration's position: "The United States admits far more foreign students than serves our national interest, and hundreds of thousands transition into a de facto guest worker program that disadvantages American graduates."

What Indian Students Should Do Now

Immigration attorneys are advising Indian students currently in the U.S. to review their program timelines and understand how the four-year cap applies to their situation. Students whose programs extend beyond four years from September 15, 2026 should prepare extension documentation early, given USCIS processing delays. Those approaching graduation should note the shortened 30-day window for post-completion decisions.

Prospective students weighing U.S. programs for fall 2027 and beyond face a fundamentally different calculation: a system that once offered open-ended flexibility now requires navigating fixed deadlines, federal extensions, and tighter restrictions on academic mobility.
nri_angle: Indian students are the largest F-1 population in the U.S. and face the steepest visa decline at 60%, with the new four-year cap and halved grace period directly threatening their academic and career plans.
